utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances today, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, all. For the Prosecution, I'm Tom Hannis, along with Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Eugene O'Sullivan, appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Aleksandar Aleksic, appearing for Zupljanin Defence. Our client is not present. He already sent a waiver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. If there are no housekeeping matters, would the usher please escort the witness back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Macar. Welcome back. We trust you're in a position to continue with us. And before I invite Mr. Zecevic to resume his examination-in-chief, I remind you that you're still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Macar.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I note that the second microphone has not been turned on. Oh, I'm ... it's going on and off.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Macar, I only have a few questions left for you and a few documents I want to show you. Let me remind you that we spoke on Friday about criminal complaints and the communication between members of the ministry and the prosecutors in 1992. The document I want to show you is 338D1, tab 96. This is a document of the basic public prosecutor's office at Kljuc. It is marked KTA 3/93 and dated 1 February 1993. It was sent to the public security station of Kljuc. It is about an event that happened at 30 July 1992, namely, the destruction of a mosque in Kljuc. It was signed by Dragan Kojic, public prosecutor. There is also a stamp. On pages 2 and 3, there's the minutes of the on-site investigation, or, rather, the on-site investigation report that was made. Are you familiar with this case, sir? The demolition of the mosque in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. At sometime in September 1993 when we analysed some problems in the territory of the Banja Luka CSB. As far as this document is concerned, I cannot tell, based on it, whether there had been a previous report by the Kljuc SJB. And in the procedural -- in the -- in the procedure, it was also the prosecutor's duty to inform the SJB or the CSB that had territorial jurisdiction if they learned about the commission of a crime and give them the relevant information. This doesn't show whether the SJB had previously submitted any report about the event in question. A request is made to the SJB to conduct additional checkups or additional investigation about the event concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what KTA stands for? In what meaning the prosecutor's office uses it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's -- KTA is the sign used for marking cases at the public prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: There's an instruction of the public prosecutor sent to the public security station. The latter is being instructed to proceed in accordance with Article 151 of the Law on Criminal Procedure. Do you remember the provisions of Article 151 of the Law on Criminal Procedure of the former SFRY which was in force at the time in the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 151 of the Law on Criminal Procedure of the former SFRY, which was transposed in the RS, dealt with the duty of the security services with regard to information about crimes or the perpetrators thereof. 153.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us take a look at page 2 now. This is a record of the on-site investigation or an on-site investigation report which was made on 30th July when the mosque was demolished. Those present were an investigating judge, a criminal inspector, a forensic technician, and a person -- another person from the prosecutor's office. I believe that you have already confirmed that you knew this crime inspector?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Gajic. And I also know the forensic technician, Mr. Gavrilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, since an on-site investigation report was made on the day of the event itself, and it says here the judge and duty was informed at 10.00 on the 30th of July, that about 0300 hours that morning, the mosque had been destroyed. Can you tell us, based on all this, if the Kljuc SJB, in fact, informed the investigating judge and forwarded the relevant documentation to the public prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Kljuc SJB informed the investigating judge which can be seen from this document and the investigative judge was in charge of the on-site investigation. Under the law, that is, the Law on Criminal Procedure, when the investigative judge goes on site, he also writes a report. He also collects information from the SJBs or CSBs that come to the site together with the investigative judge. The site must be secured previously by members of the SJB, and it was the judge's duty to make a report and submit a copy -- actually, the prosecutor's office, after the on-site investigation, requests information, especially in cases involving unknown perpetrators, and the -- the police station is required to continue working on the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Under the then-Law on Criminal Procedure, who is in charge of the investigation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the investigative judge. Only in case of minor criminal offences, such as minor crimes against property or so, investigative judges would let the security services complete the investigation in practice. But, as I said, those were mostly minor criminal offences.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Under the then-Law on Criminal Procedure, could the investigative judge and the public prosecutor give instructions to members of the MUP with regard to procure information or evidence?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were duty-bound to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I seek to tender this document, unless there are objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D659, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 339D1, tab 98.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document that contains a total of ten instructions of the basic public prosecutor's office at Kljuc sent to the public security station from 24 July 1992 through 1 February 1993. They are about various serious crimes, such as murder, rape, or other cases of violent death. Take a look, sir. You will see that there's mention made of the victims, and can you say anything about their ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most persons are Muslims. However, one person, Milomir Buljan --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure if that is the correct name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- could be a Croat. I remember the family name Buljan because there was a well-known football player by that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On page 7 in the Serbian version, there's this memo, and I suppose it's on page 3 or 4 in English. It's the last page, anyway. It says: "Regarding the murder of Milan Buljan from Ponjire." This must be a mistake. It says 13 December 1993. And since the date of the memo is 1 February 1993: "Instructions are given to proceed in accordance with Article 151 of the Law on Critical Procedure." Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a renowned football player by the name of Buljan. He was a Croat and played for a club based in Split, Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us go to page 3. There's a memo dated 10 August 1992. It's marked KTA 61/92, and signed by Dragan Kojic public prosecutor. It was sent to the Kljuc SJB. It's about the death of Alija Filipovic, which occurred on the 2nd or 3rd of August, 1992. It says: "I request that you take ... measures ... to identify the perpetrator or perpetrators, and ... file a criminal report and corroborate it with necessary evidence." There are ten such examples. Was this the usual type of communication that went on between the prosecutor's office and members of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was the usual procedure when it comes to the communication between the public prosecutor's office and the members of the MUP. The prosecutor's office is informed by means of a criminal complaint about the crime and its known or unknown perpetrator. When the criminal complaint is filed against an unknown perpetrator, this is a type of communication by which the prosecutor requests subsequent activities and the collection of material evidence about the crime and its perpetrator.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So all the events are from the time-period relevant for the indictment in 1992. With regard to the last recorded event, there must be a typo, because it says it was -- it occurred in 1993. Tell me, sir, such a written instruction from the public prosecutor, is it binding upon the MUP members?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. The same way the Law on Criminal Procedure is binding.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In a situation when either the investigative judge or the public prosecutor issues such an instruction to the bodies of the MUP, do the MUP executives, such as you who were chief of the crime enforcement administration, can you change such an instruction issued by the public prosecutor or the investigative judge?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No member of the MUP, executive or staff, can change a prosecutor's order. And they also cannot change the Law on Criminal Procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I seek to tender this document, unless there are objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D660, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, I'm going to show you a document for you to comment. We're moving onto a different topic now. 40D1, tab 77. Sir, this is a document dated 21 October 1992. It's an authorisation. In the signature block we see the typed name of the minister, Mico Stanisic. The document number is 10-2/75/92. And the minister authorises the assistant for the police, Tomo Kovac, to discharge all duties of the minister in his absence. Let me first ask you if you can tell by this number which administration drafted this document?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be the administration for analysis which typed this document up, in accordance with the order of the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is the 21st of October, 1992. Can you explain to us why this kind of authorisation was issued?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I have already given you an answer to that question, or at least part of it in my previous answers. There was some political pressure from some spheres in Republika Srpska as early as in the first half of 1992. And by October, there was an escalation and a culmination, in effect. In my opinion, I -- well, I was quite surprised to hear that the minister was transferring the authorisation, all his powers to Mr. Kovac because I thought that there would be more of an issue of assistance in the establishment of the ministry, especially in light of the fact that the headquarters of the MUP switched to Bijeljina, and there was a lot of effort to set up the organisational units and to step up the activities in the field to set up the chain of command. Unfortunately, the pressure really escalated from the government and some of the political circles, and this is why this gentleman, in fact, why the minister transferred the powers onto Mr. Kovac, empowering him to carry on the activities in the Ministry of the Interior. I think that quite soon Mr. Stanisic, indeed, was removed from office. And I would like to add here that the MUP headquarters in Bijeljina were set up in rather peculiar circumstances because of the pressure exerted by the political circles on the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, when you say political pressure from some actors or players in Republika Srpska, you did say right at the beginning that in October there was a culmination of those pressures. Could you please tell us what political circles did you have in mind? Or, rather, first, tell me, was the pressure exerted on the minister and the ministry?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was aimed at the minister himself but also on the ministry. And as I've already said, it started by Mr. Djeric, and it culminated, it was orchestrated by Ms. Plavsic, who was a member of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what was behind this pressure that was first exerted by Mr. Djeric and was later orchestrated by Ms. Plavsic, as a member of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that some individuals in the executive branch of the government and who were in power could not really find their bearings in the beginning of the war. And they were not familiar with the civil service that they were supposed to establish. Here, I'm primarily referring to Mr. Djeric. And in the course of 1992, the Ministry of the Interior and the minister demanded from the government to assist them in setting up the ministry, but also to assist in setting up the other bodies which were required for the ministry to function properly. Otherwise everything was in vain. And, now, as to why Ms. Plavsic joined in this campaign, I don't know. But I think that she took at face value some of the information that came in from some municipalities, in particular, in the Sarajevo region, where the ministry was trying to place under its control, or, rather, to prevent the theft of property from some businesses and to prevent the unlawful disposition of this property. And from these areas, misinformation came into the ministry, and the ministry ended up being accused of all the misdeeds that happened in each and every municipality. And now this all came together with what Mr. Djeric was saying, and there were constant attacks practically each and every month on Mr. Stanisic. It escalated to parody, you could say. With the arrival in Bijeljina, because of this pressure, the situation arose where the senior officers in Bijeljina could not say who the personnel that was supposed to set up the ministry were, what they were all about. Most of the Serbian last names end in "ic." I have to explain this for your benefit, Your Honours. But we had five or six senior officers, Macar, Zuba, Kovac, and so on, and those circles launched pressure which spread to the public, and the public demanded the MUP to check who we are, what our ethnic background was. So the pressure went all the way down to the grassroots level, from the very top levels of the political life.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you know at what assembly Mr. Djeric's cabinet fell? At what session of the assembly did all the ministers resign?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in November 1992. Well, I can't really be more specific about that. I attended most of the sessions of the assembly between 1992 and 1995 because there were always some items on the agenda that had to do with the work of the MUP, and the MUP representatives had to be present there to report. In the course of my attendance to those assembly sessions, I became aware of the work of some of the deputies who were instructed to intervene, to speak, in order to exert pressure on the ministry and the minister. And here I am speaking about the pressure exerted or originating from Ms. Plavsic. I, in fact, got most of my information from those deputies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall being present in November 1992 at this session of the assembly in Zvornik when the government fell?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not in Zvornik. It is one of the few assembly sessions that I did not attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about the conflict between Ms. Plavsic and Minister Stanisic that pertained the -- to the volunteers and groups that came into Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about this conflict. The position of the MUP and of the Republika Srpska army, once it was established, was that, in organisational terms, all the armed forces had to be under the control of the Ministry of Defence. Or, rather, that all the army personnel had to be under their command. But Ms. Plavsic, acting on her own initiative, this was probably in the course of her visits to Belgrade, to visit her relatives, she would get in touch with various people, and she arranged for the volunteers to come. And we mostly had security problems because of those volunteers, and Republika Srpska army had most of those problems because it had to try to place them under their control. They also caused problems for the municipalities where they arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document, unless there are any objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There is an objection, Your Honour. This document does not have a signature. It does not have a stamp. So there's no indication that it came from the minister. Based on the number, this witness says it comes from the analytical section and he said it was probably typed up by someone from there. But we have no indication whether or not this was a final document, whether it was actually implemented. The appropriate person would be someone from that administration, perhaps Mr. Kovac, or perhaps whoever actually authored the document. But from this witnesses has added, you don't have sufficient basis to admit this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: My query, Mr. Zecevic, would have been that we have the witness's testimony as to the political goings-on that occurred at this time, and this document doesn't -- it's almost a footnote. Do we really need it, apart from the points that Mr. Hannis has made?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I -- I disagree with the points which Mr. Hannis was making because of the witness's testimony, and I can elaborate on that. But if Your Honours feel it is not required, then I do agree it is just to support the witness's testimony. This document is just to support witness's testimony. But if Your Honours are satisfied with the testimony as sufficient for this -- for this point, I don't insist on -- on introducing this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to add the document says that the ministry authorises Mr. Kovac to perform all ministerial duties on his behalf, in his absence. There is no indication of whether his absence is referring to an absence for two hours that afternoon, for the rest of 1992, or for what period at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. Zecevic, the Chamber wouldn't necessarily take on board your comments about being satisfied because that suggests a conclusion which would be premature for us. But, basically, we understand what you are saying and treat your comment as -- as a withdrawal of your application to tender the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise, Your Honours. I didn't mean to suggest anything of the kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Of course, not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, are you familiar with this document, and are you familiar with the situation; and, if so, how?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I tried to say something a little while ago to assist you. Yes, I am familiar with this document. I saw it in Bijeljina, the original, signed and certified by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, it has been brought to our attention that the witness may have been trying to indicate something to the Chamber? Mr. Macar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, I violated the procedure. I tried to say something into the microphone while you were conferring regarding this document. Let me explain the procedure, how documents were drafted. I was able to see the original signed and certified, and the documents were usually done in three copies. This copy was used in order for the person who actually took receipt of the original document. And it is indicated here 21st of October, 1992, personally received by Mr. Mitrovic. He was Mr. Kovac's driver. He took receipt of the certified document. And this is why this copy is not signed. It is usually kept in the analysis administration, in its files. And the original was kept in legal and personnel administration, certified and stamped. This is a document that simply proves that somebody took receipt of the original signed and certified document, which I was able to see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I have to ask you again because of the comments made by my learned friend, what was the reason, very briefly and concisely, for this kind of authorisation to be issued to Tomo Kovac?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main reason was the political pressure and other kinds of pressure. That was the basic reason why the minister delegated his authority to Mr. Kovac, or, rather, transferred his powers on Mr. Kovac, so that Mr. Kovac could continue being in charge of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a few questions, sir. I'm hoping that we should be able, by the end of the first session ... Did you receive any kind of decoration in 1993 or 1994 when decorations were awarded by the Republika Srpska -- by the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the procedure of awarding decorations; and who was it that awarded them?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The nominations for decorations came from the local communities, the local authorities. Then, in case of members of the VRS, they came from the organisational units of the army. And there were also other public authorities involved. The idea of awarding decorations originated due to an intention that individuals should be acknowledged for their contributions to the -- to the public good, especially members of the army. But some organisations nominated individuals of doubtful qualities. All these nominations were submitted to a commission that was to check them and narrow down the circle of candidates. But given the war time conditions, it was questionable to what extent they were able to really do their job. It was my position back in 1993, and it hasn't changed since, I was also nominated for a decoration, the Karadjordjevo Star of the Second Order, and I said even then that my name shouldn't have been on that list because there were people who had done much more than I. The basic idea of decorating persons was to acknowledge the bravest and to pay tribute to the fallen members of the armed forces. And 782 police officers got killed in that war. If we add to that number the hundreds of wounded and disabled, especially in 1992 and 1993, the use of MUP members, that is, police officers and the armed forces, was out of proportion. For all these reason, all these people deserve to be decorated much more than I. As I said, that was my position back then, and is hasn't changed since.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You have explained that - if I understood correctly - the initiative was with the local authorities.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to a great extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: With regard to VRS members, who was it that nominated persons to be decorated?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It all originated from the commands of lower-ranking units, and it went up the ladder.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, and here's my last question for you, sir. I believe that it was at the beginning of your testimony that you said to us that you met -- that you first met Mr. Stanisic in 1977 or 1978 when you took up employment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So by 1992 you had known him for 15 years, and you co-operated in 1992. Tell us your opinion about Mr. Stanisic, sir, especially with regard to his attitude toward members of other ethnicities or members of other peoples from the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I haven't had the opportunity to do so when replying to a previous question, let me say now that Mr. Stanisic was held in high esteem in police circles as a good professional. He was very disciplined and a model officer. From the time I first met him, to his two terms in office as minister, he never once, in a meeting or outside, said anything bad against non-Serbian citizens. I never heard anything of the kind. Before the war, he worked for companies where he was in a managerial position, and in those companies there were also members of other ethnicities. I heard that he had -- he was on friendly terms with non-Serbs and had friends among them. I have never heard Mr. Stanisic say anything bad about non-Serbs, in spite of the war and anything that occurred then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And here's my last question: Given the fact that you co-operated with Mr. Stanisic, especially in 1992 and during his second term in office in 1994, tell us about Mr. Stanisic's attitude toward crime.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already pointed out, Mr. Stanisic was, first and foremost, a police officer. Even as a minister, he wasn't a politician. He was a professional police officer. His attitude towards everybody and especially towards crimes committed during the war, was always the same: He insisted that every crime should be solved and no distinctions should be made between crimes. Never could one feel at a collegium or any other meeting that Mr. Stanisic had double criteria, and I'm certain that he still feels the same today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Macar. No more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So that conveniently brings us to the first break. And we would hear from Mr. Krgovic when we return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning again, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Macar.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, we have already met some ten days ago. We met briefly. This is just for the record. My name is Dragan Krgovic. I am Defence counsel for Mr. Zupljanin, and I'm about to ask you some questions about your testimony so as far, as well as some things you have already discussed with Mr. Zecevic. Let me first ask you for some clarification. You mentioned the name of a forensic technician from Banja Luka. That person is Vilko Maric.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: He's a Croat by ethnicity, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And as far as I understood you, he worked at the forensic centre in Banja Luka in 1992. Later, he moved onto the newly established centre in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, Mr. Vilko Maric worked for the forensic department in the crime enforcement section of the Banja Luka CSB. And in 1993, when the ministry established a forensic centre in Banja Luka, which, in organisational terms, was a subunit of the crime police administration, Mr. Maric was transferred to that forensics centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Just a bit more clarification. In 1992, all the staff of the forensic centre in Banja Luka were actually members of the Banja Luka CSB. And in 1993, when the centre was established as a separate organisational unit, they became members of that separate organisational unit of the MUP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And if I may explain, some of the forensic staff from the centre were transferred to the forensic centre which was an organisational unit of the crime enforcement administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And, in 1992, this staff that was transferred were tasked to conduct on-site investigations or secure a crime site, and they were issued orders to do so by some senior crime enforcement officers; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forensic department of the CSB was ordered, or, actually, received orders from its superiors at the Banja Luka CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And, in 1993, the situation changed somewhat, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In 1993, the forensics centre was an organisational unit of the crime enforcement administration of the ministry itself. That was a -- that was an organisational unit in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And, in 1992, if one of the people working there, such as Brane Buhovac, had to go somewhere and carry out an investigative measure, they received orders to do so from Stojan Zupljanin or Djuro Bulic; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the system of subordination, the forensic department had above it the chief of the crime enforcement section and then, further up, the chief of the centre, upon whose request they had to act.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And up until 1993, they didn't receive orders from your service. It had to go through a centre, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Almost until the end of 1992, we didn't have functioning communication, nor was the administration able to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just like most of the staff of the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, you will have to repeat because the interpreters were unable to follow you. My question was: Up until 1993, they couldn't receive instructions or orders from your service, but because the -- in that respect, they were under the Banja Luka CSB; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In brief, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to clarify. When you were answering Mr. Zecevic's question, you were referring to two periods, one before the end of 1992, and the other, starting in 1993. Mr. Macar, I can see that you are in distress. If you should at any moment feel that you cannot continue, we can have an earlier break.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we can continue. For the time being, I can still find a position that I can bear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In your previous testimony, you touched upon some topics that I would like to discuss with you now. That's why I gave you some documents which partly deal with the things you spoke about. So please take a look at tab 2 in your binder. And the exhibit is P624. Answering Mr. Zecevic's question, you mentioned various sources of information that you received and your familiarity with the situation on the ground. One of the ways the ministry learned about the work of the individual centres was through periodical and annual reports; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please go to page 7 of this document, which is page 4 in English. Actually, it is marked 6 on the hard copy; whereas, it's 7 in e-court. Mr. Macar, do take a look at footnote 1 at the bottom of page 6. It mentions the personnel strength of the MUP. I'm interested in the following information: On 31 December 1992, there was a total of 1.203 activity duty and 5.065 reserve policemen in the territory of the Banja Luka CSB which, if my math is correct, totals 6.288 members. Please go back to page 2 in hard copy, which is page 2 in English as well. Now there is something here that I want to discuss with you. In line 7 from the top, the participation of MUP members in the war is mentioned. It says: "... 5.34 employees were engaged in combat operations for 114.529 days." You said that, as far as you knew, the percentage of police officers taking part in combat operations was up to 70 or 80 per cent. You remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And if we look at 6.288 employees, about 5.000 of them took part, that would be about 60 [as interpreted] per cent of the overall strength who took part in the combat operations in the Banja Luka CSB area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry, I do apologise. I said 80 per cent, or 80.1 per cent, according to my calculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Macar, you will agree that such a high percentage of employees who took part in combat operations affected substantially the security situation in the Banja Luka CSB area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not only the security situation in the Banja Luka CSB, but in all the other centres as well. And if we add to this, that by the end of the year, there were only 1.200 -- 100, 1.200 active-duty policemen; in other words, people who had some experience in the security tasks. And the Banja Luka CSB had 24 public security stations within its area. And out of the 24 SJBs, to the best of my recollection, at least 16 were in the combat area, or, rather, bordered on the areas where combat operations were ongoing. And the massive participation of the security services personnel in the combat operations affected the security situation definitely, and also affected the quality of work of the public security stations.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at page 2 in this document. In e-court, in the Serbian, that would be page 3, and page 2 in the English version. Well, as in all the reports that we have seen, we have the basic characteristics of the security situation and public law and order, and you spoke about that in answer to my colleague Mr. Zecevic's questions. I will now read this part so that you can see whether this corresponds to the knowledge that you gained through the reports or from other sources when you visited the ground. And it says here that a characteristic for the situation is the conduct of combat operations in various areas. And then it goes on to say about some organisational issues. And then it says repeated disturbances of law and order and inability to maintain it, and to -- there's a danger that this might go out of control, physical and armed attacks on the police officers, unauthorised use of weapons, lack of compliance with the law, and increasing levels of civil disobedience, a decrease in the level of social tolerance, spreading of rumours and disinformation, an increase in the most serious forms of crime, brigandry, causing of general danger, general sense of insecurity, poverty, and the precarious social conditions for a growing number of people. Mr. Macar, you will agree with me that this situation prevailed not only in the Banja Luka CSB but -- or, rather, that it prevailed in the whole of the Banja Luka area?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, based on the reports, the situation was almost the same. Well, the same, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you not about Banja Luka as -- but Republika Srpska as a whole.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I actually meant. It was the same throughout Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at page 5 in e-court. That's page 6 in the Serbian version and page 4 in the English version. Mr. Zecevic asked you a number of questions and showed you a number of documents about some crimes that were committed by people in uniform. And let me read this passage to you, and I would like to ask you whether this tallies with your knowledge? That's the second paragraph, that says: "In an atmosphere of radical deterioration of the security situation, which keeps getting more complex, there has been a marked escalation of crime ... by armed groups and individuals of Serbian ethnicity who tend to deny the authority and block the work of legal government organs. The criminal activity of criminal groups and individuals creates an impression of anarchy and lawlessness in the public ... which seriously undermines the reputation of the legal government institutions and creates distrust in them, especially because some of these groups and criminals use uniforms and the insignia of the army and police of Republika Srpska when committing their [sic] crimes." And then there is a description of the crimes they commit. And then it goes on to say: "Another security problem is the operation of groups and individuals of Serbian ethnicity aimed at seizing power in an illegal manner." Mr. Macar, you know that in some municipalities there were some groups, wearing all kinds of uniforms, actually had power throughout 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some groups were in power and a number of them tried to use violence, in order to influence the existing government bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me now show you a part that has to do with crime. Could you please look at page 9, page 10 in e-court, and page 6 in the English version. That would be more of your purview. Mr. Macar, the first paragraph about the number of criminal complaints submitted in the Banja Luka area, in answer to Mr. Zecevic's question, you spoke about criminal complaints that were filed against unidentified perpetrators. And here we have a figure that unidentified perpetrators committed --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The percentage is 47.3 per cent of crimes that were not solved. Well, the percentage of solved crimes, if you compare it with the some other periods before and after the war or with other countries, how would you describe it, as satisfactory or not satisfactory?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, even in peacetime conditions this would be a considered a satisfactory number of crimes solved, if you are talking about crimes committed by unidentified perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And in this report we can see that these are crimes that are being committed systematically and that are not typical of peacetime conditions: Arson, torching, mass murders, aggravated robberies, and so on; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And all CSBs and all SJBs, not just the centre in Banja Luka, faced this kind of problem for the first time, in effect, of -- once the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that when Mr. Zecevic asked me a question, I said that the MUP personnel of -- the personnel of the MUP of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina did not have adequate training to act in a civil, ethnic-based war, especially in a war where everybody had weapons and when crimes were so widespread, theft, robbery, murders, and so on. The police suddenly had to operate to act against armed criminal groups whose equipment were superior, in some cases, to military equipment and weapons. And also, the rugged terrain was another tactor. The number of Security Services Centre personnel involved in the war, which meant that the number of operatives in the field went down. In the initial stages, this all affected the sharp rise in crime. And it took quite some time for the ministry and for the SJBs to adapt to this new situation. One of the main reasons, as I've already said in my previous answers, for the minister to give this order to transform the special unit into a special detachment that would be operating at the regional level, the reason was that we wanted to have this kind of force to assist the regular police in maintaining the security situation at acceptable levels. I have to apologise if I was too broad in my explanations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at paragraph 3, or, rather the third paragraph in this report again on this page, where it says -- well, you spoke at length to my colleague, Mr. Zecevic, about the crimes and the criminal complaints that were filed for murder in the first degree. Well, they could be qualified as war crimes or murders. But here it says that some criminal complaints were filed for the crime -- crimes against humanity and public law, and some municipalities are mentioned here: Teslic and Knezevo SJBs. Knezevo, where is that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Skender Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I spoke too fast. Teslic and Knezevo. So, Mr. Macar, do you know that the criminal complaint for Koricanske Stijene which are in the Knezevo SJB territory, whether there are any other complaints were filed for the war crime that may have happened there in 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know there was some crimes in Teslic where criminal complaints were filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: That would be the Mice Group?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's what they were called. That was their nickname, Mice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But the criminal complaint for Koricanske Stijene in the Knezevo SJB?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The complaint for Koricanske Stijene was filed initially a crime by unidentified perpetrators and action was taken to identify the perpetrators. Since the perpetrators were wearing police uniform, probably those were reserve police officers from Prijedor. That's what was discovered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You were explaining to Mr. Zecevic that when you arrived in 1993, you were informed that they had joined the VRS and that measures were being taken to find them; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that. There was information that a number of perpetrators had been identified - I don't know now if there were two or three of them identified - and that these persons had joined a VRS unit, and that measures were being taken to identify and locate them in order to bring them in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please move onto page 24 in your version. It's page 25 in e-court and Serbian. And page 14 in English. Mr. Macar, the second paragraph from the top, you have just said or told -- told us about the problems the police was facing at the time: A shortage of staff, and especially police staff, to work under difficult conditions. That was a significant factor affecting the work of the police, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: An assessment made by Mr. Zupljanin in his report is that the impression is created that the situation is -- or, rather, that the authorities are losing control over the situation. The ineffectiveness of the security organs and services in carrying out the duties envisaged by law which is primarily reflected in the slow processing of the crimes, that was a problem that prevailed in the entire territory of the RS, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Answering Mr. Zecevic's question, you also spoke about the roles of Crisis Staffs. I'm going to read out the following paragraph to you, which is on the following page in English. The inefficiency, unprofessional attitude, has contributed to ... "... the ineffectiveness, lack of professionalism, and negligence in the work of a number of SJB staff is largely a result of the functional and operational independence of a number of SJBs from the centre which is greatly undermined the overall unity and social role of the security organs and services." What does that mean, Mr. Macar, "functional and operational"? Could you please explain?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Individual SJB senior officers, some of whom didn't have previous experience in policing, organised their work in such a way that Crisis Staffs or some circles in the municipal authorities were actually running and directing the SJBs. And a practice spread that the Crisis Staff, rather than the CSB, was their superior body, which means that they weren't really in the chain of subordination of the MUP. That's how the functional system of security was disappearing. That was certainly not in line with the Law on Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And, as we see in the following sentence: "... some of these SJBs link their activities to local politics and local political leaders, neglecting their legal obligations and authority."

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please move onto the following page, which is page 25 in your binder, 26 in e-court, and 15 in the English version. I'm interested in the second paragraph where Mr. Zupljanin discusses this problem and says: "A number of SJBs ignores the centre's requests for information on certain issues and fails to react promptly to certain requests ... thus jeopardising the unity of the security organs and services and their ability to operate as a single security system. In such circumstances, it is very difficult to have the overall security situation under control and ... assess and make valid security assessments and estimates. Thus, by becoming independent, the SJBs inevitably undermine the integral security system of the region and the Republic; that is, they brought into question the integral function of the security organs and services and weakened the entire defence" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: "Protection system."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, this is a realistic picture of the security system, not only of the Banja Luka region but the entire RS in 1992, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring only to this paragraph or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I pointed out this part about the security system.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, the problems are -- with some SJBs are related in an analytical manner. Those problems were caused by the chiefs of those SJBs, especially those who had not been appointed by the MUP or nominated by the Security Services Centre. The Banja Luka centre, at other centres, had very little influence on that. There were such cases in other centres, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And, specifically, answering Mr. Zecevic's question, you pointed out Prijedor as a typical example of an SJB breaking loose from both the Security Services Centre and the MUP.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I was shocked by the -- by the extent of that problem. By the scope of that problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, I'm just being informed that not your entire reply was recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You were shocked by the scope of the problem and what else? The non-recognition of the centre and the ministry on the part of the people in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I literally said not only by the extent of disrespect but also by the lack of knowledge or ignorance of the role of the ministry headquarters. Toilet?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have anything to say, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I think we would take the break a little early and come back in 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: While the witness is on his way in, we'll take the next break at 12.30, and then after 15 minutes, we will be back, more or less, on track.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In your reply recorded on page 31, lines 17 through 19, you mention disrespect and ignorance of the role of the ministry headquarters and added -- you also added a -- of the centres, too. Didn't you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I said it twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And when you say "centres," you mean the Banja Luka CSB?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Banja Luka CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, take a look at page 26 in your binder, which is 27 in e-court, and it's page 15 of the English translation. In this first paragraph, some things are dealt with that you discussed with Mr. Zecevic, that control should be introduced over these members of the MUP that didn't abide by the regulations? And in the following paragraph, we see that it says, "Out of" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot see the relevant section in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's at the bottom of the page, continuing on page 16 in English. I will read it again for the interpreters: "Certain duties envisaged by the law were not carried out because of fear and apprehension, and in some cases because of involvement in various criminal affairs. And there were attempts to shift responsibility to others and even to the centre."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, this especially applied to Prijedor, wasn't it, and especially after the removal of Mr. Drljaca, when he was trying to present things in such a manner as to clear him from any responsibility; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at another document, Mr. Macar. It's in tab 1. That's P595. Mr. Macar, in addition to this annual report in the pre-war times, the practice was to file periodical repots, depending on the needs, whether of the SJBs or the Security Services Centres.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the practice was to file reports every three month, six months, and the annual reports, or, on demand, whenever the Ministry of the Interior or the public security department requested that reports be filed at other times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at page -- the next page, in effect, introductory remarks. Look at the footnote, number 1: "The report from the centre was supposed to contain the reports of the SJBs to incorporated all the reports of the SJBs." That was the principle?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The centre's reports were based on the activities of the SJBs and the centre itself in the headquarters for those tasks that were within their purview.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Let me quote from the footnote where it says: "Furthermore, some of the SJBs, despite the insistence from the centre and despite exceeding all the deadlines, have not filed their reports by the 27th of July, 1991 [as interpreted], as they were supposed to." And then there's a list of municipalities that did not file their reports and two of them are in -- listed in the indictment, Skender Vakuf and Donji Vakuf. That probably has a number of causes, Mr. Macar, but this speaks to the fact that, as we have already discussed, that some SJBs became, de facto, independent of the centre and of the ministry; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that can be a cause.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a correction. Page 34, line 5, the date is the 27th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And then the centre states in the report that the quality of the reports is rather low in terms of the analysis, and it does not correspond to the circumstances and the situation. Mr. Zupljanin is insisting here that the centre itself was unable to determine what was really going on, on the ground for a number of reasons, of course. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in many public security stations, as I've already indicated, there was a lack of trained personnel, personnel who would be able to perform all of their tasks. And that is why even the periodical reports boiled down to some statistical data and there was no appropriate analysis of the security situation of each and every security factor. It was just barest statistics. There was no assessment of the situation from the station itself. They did not describe the situation, and they did not describe the measures taken or justify failure to take measures. They did not specify their plans to deal with their own failures and defects and also to deal with the problems on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, could you please move on to page 11 in the hard copy. That would be page 8 in the English version, and I believe that in e-court, that would be page 9, or, rather, page 12 in the Serbian. So the English version, I believe, is page 8. Mr. Zecevic asked you about some instances where buildings were torched, some explosions, and so on. And I would like to bring your attention to what Mr. Zupljanin highlights here as a problem, where he is speaking about the criminal activities of groups and individuals, and the combat operations. And then he goes on to say that there are instances of unauthorised entry into citizens' apartments, blowing up socially owned and privately owned buildings. And then he says, in paragraph 3: "These activities have caused anger and resentments, mainly among the Serbian people in whose name and with whose symbols heinous criminal acts, looting, arson, and violence, are being committed. Fear is generated among other ethnic groups which inevitably brings about ethnic divisions and distrust in the institutions of the systems -- of the system." Mr. Macar, Mr. Zupljanin obviously is saying what all of you in the ministry must have noted, how all those activities impacted on the security station in Republika Srpska as a whole.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most of those phenomenon often led the minister to issue various instructions and guide-lines how to deal with those acts more efficiently and effectively and also to co-operate better with the relevant military organs in order to suppress such actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We will wait, Mr. Macar, for this part of your answer to be recorded. In your reply, you said that these actions prompted the minister, led the minister, and that's not recorded.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the minister issued instructions and orders to the people on the ground, demanding that more vigorous action be taken by the public security sections and the CSBs to fight these kinds of activities and to establish links with the relevant security organs in the military, in order to keep them informed and to take joint action to fight these kind of activities and to create a more favourable security situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, could you please move to page 24 in the hard copy that you have in front of you. In e-court, it is 25 in the Serbian version, and 16 in the English version. Please read the last paragraph and then we will move onto the next page. That would be page 26 in the e-court, in the Serbian version, your version, that's page 25. And we're still on the same page in the English language where it is indicated that there should be co-operation between the military and the organs of the Ministry of the Interior. This is what you have been saying; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you talked with Mr. Zecevic, you spoke about a number of factors that affected the solve rate of the crimes. Let me read the next paragraph on page 25 where it says: "Major problems for the services in this situation are caused by the refusal of the citizens to co-operate. The avoidance of officials and some mistrust and the passive role of the operative stronghold, so that the initial data collected can be checked with some difficulty which affects the accuracy of assessments of the social threat posed by security-related developments and events." Mr. Macar, each and every polices force in the world has some informers, some sources, and it depends on the trust of the citizens in order to be able to do its job and detect crimes. Now, once the war broke out in Republika Srpska, this situation changed. It was upside down.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a characteristic for the entire Republika Srpska, not only for the Banja Luka CSB area. There was fear, which is only natural if you are in a war. And criminal groups and armed individuals who committed crimes were rampant, and people were reluctant to come forward and report some things they knew to the public security station personnel. At our meetings, I always demanded that more vigorous action be taken by the crime police. I was speaking as the chief of the crime police department. And those who felt some fear, who were too afraid to work, should leave the crime police. And I also had some understanding for the fear of the citizens for their personal safety that they faced if they decided to come forward, and that is something that was present in each and every municipality in Republika Srpska. And I don't even have to talk about those small villages where everybody is related to everyone else. And, of course, the war exacerbated this situation, and the situation this those small villages was even worse than it was in the larger centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Even the victims who survived some crimes were reluctant to testify against the perpetrators because they feared for their safety; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that it was a general phenomenon, based on the flow of information that we received from the victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, there is a sentence here in this paragraph which reads: "The real nature of the security assessments is affected by lack of information and co-ordination between the centre, the public security stations, and the Ministry of the Interior and other CSBs in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Do you agree with me, and do you agree what Mr. Zupljanin says here that there was no co-ordination between the CSBs, the SJBs, and the Ministry of the Interior, at least in this period that Mr. Zupljanin is talking about here?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would like to say, first of all, that this lack of communication between the stations, the centres, and the ministry itself, and this inability to respond promptly on the part of the ministry, primarily for technical reasons, especially at the beginning of the war, that it caused greater problems for the ministry itself in the headquarters, because they did not have information. They did not get information promptly about what was going on, on the ground. And then, based on this information, they were supposed to take specific measures and issue instructions to the relevant areas. The public security stations were duty-bound to operate in line with the Law on the Internal Affairs and the Law on Criminal Procedure. The CSB, likewise, had to do that. Because of the difficulties that we have already described, at the beginning of the war, in particular, the flow of information was irregular, the flow of information from the stations to the centres. And the centres themselves did not really know what was going on in each and every segment of the security sector in the territories covered by the public security stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Here, at the bottom, Mr. Zupljanin says, when it comes to the Banja Luka CSB: "All forms of self-organising parallel bodies of the government, self-contained territories of various types on various bases, terror and violence against the population, and armed conflict and general anarchy and chaos." And then further on, as regards the security services personnel, he notes that this puts them in the difficulty situation and makes it very difficult for them to carry out their legal tasks, i.e., guaranteeing the public law and order, and security for the citizens and their property. Do you agree, Mr. Macar, that in those days, when the conflict broke out in April, and then, later on, in 1992, that this actually applied to the whole of Republika Srpska, and that the position of the MUP personnel, because of this, was very difficult and that they could not do their job as they were duty-bound under the law?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In numerous municipalities, the civilian authorities and also the military authorities were at a loss. We're talking about Crisis Staffs, a new practice came into being, that they were the most responsible and that they had the right to manage all the structures, including the security services. Those who had been with the MUP longer, who had had more experience, were able to bypass these pitfalls. But the -- those with less experience became the servants of these authorities. And the Crisis Staffs affected the way the SJBs functioned greatly. They practically issued instructions and orders to the SJBs which was in direct contravention of the Law on Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, I have no more questions of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, my name is Tom Hannis. I'm a Prosecutor. I understand that you have been experiencing some difficulties during your time here, and I just wanted to indicate that if any time you feel like you need a break sooner than the scheduled time, please let us know. And with the Judge's permission, I would tell you that if it is urgent, and you don't feel like you have time to wait for the translation, just hold up your hand and start out of the room, and we'll understand. I don't want you to suffer because it takes time for the message to get through. I wanted to begin with what Mr. Zecevic started, but I guess while we are just finished with Mr. Krgovic, I will ask you a couple of questions about that. Mr. Krgovic said that the two of you had met some ten days ago. Was that the first and only time that you met with anybody from the Zupljanin Defence team?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how long did you meet with Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't really time it, but it wasn't a long meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Did he show you any documents in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, we spoke more about some procedural matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you show him any documents that you might have had?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. With regard to Mr. Stanisic, Mico Stanisic's Defence team, when did you first become aware that you were going to be asked to be a witness for Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember the exact time and date. I know that after being interviewed by your investigators, I was asked and explained that I may become a Prosecution witness in this trial. I know that some colleagues of mine had already been called in that capacity. And I think that Mr. Zecevic's assistant informed me over the phone that I was on their list of Defence witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I have copies of -- of some notes of an interview or a meeting that I think Mr. Zecevic or somebody from his Defence team had with you in March of this year. Do you recall meeting with them and being interviewed or discussing your possible testimony in this case?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't speak about the case in March, but I was informed, but I can't say when exactly, that I was short-listed as a Defence witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before coming here to The Hague for your testimony last week and this week, did you have a meeting with Mr. Zecevic or anyone from the Defence team to go over documents and discuss the content of your anticipated testimony; and, if so, when and where was that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic's assistant, whose name I now forget, informed me that I was scheduled for the 20th of June. I was summoned when I had some medical problems, and I remember that the correspondence went back and forth five or six times. I was explaining -- or, rather, I was explained what had to be done, and so on and so forth, but then I ended up in the emergency ward for some urgent checkups.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My question is: Did you have a face-to-face meeting with anybody from Mr. Zecevic's team, Mr. Stanisic's Defence team, during this year, 2011? Not counting your proofing here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember seeing anybody on Mr. Zecevic's team this year. I may have seen Mr. Cvijetic in passing, in Bijeljina, but we didn't really know each other, nor did we communicate. So even if I did pass him, or meet him on the street, I didn't say hello.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, did you have a -- did you have an interview over the telephone with the person who contacted you on behalf of Mr. Stanisic's team? Because I have a document that's uploaded into e-court, the document ERN is 1D07-0138 through 0144, and I thought there was a notation on that document indicating it was from March of 2011. So if you didn't have a face-to-face meeting, did you have a discussion on the phone, an interview, if you will, about the contents of your anticipated testimony?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We'll come back to that later then. When --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]... I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, there was not -- there was no original, if you wanted to show the document to the witness. There was no original on the -- on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will come back to it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you --

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, if I may have just a minute to go to the toilet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps to save some time with the witness, maybe I could ask the Court to ask of Defence counsel if they could provide me with some guidance on this document, which we received as being a statement or notes of an interview with Mr. Macar, and I don't recall where I got it, but -- it was my understanding it was from March 2011. It's not signed by the witness, so I'm not clear on the provenance. It was loaded by the Defence, and I can use some assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this -- this document is, to my recollection, from March, but can I find out the precise date when it was received. It was an e-mail sent by Mr. Macar to us, concerning the -- the issues that we discussed during -- during the previous meeting that I had with him. I hope this is ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's a start. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, are you okay to go on to our next scheduled break at 12.30?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, we do have a document on the screen. I don't know if you can see the B/C/S version. I have some information now that suggests to me that perhaps -- is this an e-mail that you may have sent to Mr. Zecevic sometime earlier this year?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know exactly when. The questions to which I provided answers were received from Mr. Cvijetic, I think. And I sent them to their office in Belgrade. I got them on the phone, but I can't give you a precise point in time, and this is a bit difficult for me to look at. It's much easier to work with hard copies, if you have any.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will, later on, come to that, and then I'll provide you a hard copy. For now, I just wanted to establish when that was created and who it came from. Now I understand this is -- this is your own written work that you sent as an e-mail in response to some questions that you had received earlier from the Stanisic Defence team; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And, as I said, we'll deal with that later. I want to go back to the beginning of your testimony last week on the 5th of July. Mr. Zecevic began about asking you about the situation just shortly before the conflict broke out in April of 1992. At transcript page 22.808, you mentioned how, in the -- in the joint MUP, I will call it, of Bosnia, there was, what you referred to, as a purge. And you explained that term as referring to the situation where certain people in leading positions were removed from those leading positions in the ministry. And you said this started with the public security stations and then went all the way up to the very top of the ministry. One of my questions related to that was, this wasn't just a matter of one ethnicity replacing another one; right? It wasn't necessarily a matter of a Serb being replaced by a Muslim, or a Muslim being replaced by a Croat, or a Croat being replaced by a Serb. I mean, I understand that did happen sometimes. But sometimes, it was happening that a Serb might be replaced by another Serb. You're aware of situations like that happening in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Speaking about the city Secretariat of the Interior in Sarajevo, I do not know of cases when a Serb was appointed to a position which was earmarked for a Muslim. And in the newly created situation, especially in the uniformed police, maybe even over 40 per cent of the employees were Serbs. Because that was simply due to the numbers in which the individual groups responded to -- to calls. As a consequence of the 1991 census, the structure was somewhat corrected, through early retirement, which was possible at the time, or, in some cases, due to changes in the job classification.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned that at the beginning of your testimony. But the point I'm asking about wasn't a real part of the problem, not so much the ethnicity of the replacement, but the qualification of the replacement. For example, in Bijeljina, before the war, it's my understanding that Mico Davidovic had been the chief in the SJB in Bijeljina. And he had been a professional policeman for some years before that. And he was replaced by Predrag Jesuric, a lawyer, who was, as I understand it, a founder and a member of the local SDS with no prior police experience. Isn't that an example of the problem where political appointees with no professional police experience were being put into these jobs throughout Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember that Mr. Davidovic was chief of the Bijeljina SJB. I think that he was chief of a local police station somewhere in the surroundings of Bijeljina. And from that position, he moved on to a unit of the federal MUP, which, given his disposition and the way he perceived of the service, was probably something that suited him well. And Mr. Jesuric was, indeed, a lawyer, who had taken his bar exam, but I don't remember which qualifications made Mr. Davidovic eligible for some higher-ranking position in the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You've talked a lot about the problems of the independence of certain SJBs in 1992, due, in part, as you said, because of their appointment by the local Crisis Staffs. And part of the problem was many of those persons appointed to be SJB chiefs did not have prior experience as policeman; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated that there were some SJB chiefs without prior experience with the MUP. And I spoke about the influence the Crisis Staffs had on some SJBs, or a considerable number, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You know Malko Koroman, who was the SJB chief in Pale for a time in 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know what he did prior to his appointment as a SJB chief in Pale? Was he a professional policeman before that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You testified on -- on the 5th of July about the 40 per cent of Serbs, you said, working in the MUP and how they tended to apply more for the uniform jobs. And then you went on to talk about the problem of -- in Sarajevo, of the number of Muslims being taken on as reserve policemen. You said many of those were Muslim citizens from Sandzak. How many people are you talking about? Are you talking about dozens, or hundreds, or thousands? Do you have a number?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
