utterances.text: You mean the number of Sandzak citizens who became reserve police officers in the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dozens. I can give you an illustration. In front of my courtyard, there were always a number of reserve police officers who hailed from Sandzak which is a territory in the east of Montenegro or on the south of Serbia. They are conspicuous by their accent. The SUP of the centre of Sarajevo which was only a few buildings away from my courtyard, had many such police officers, and our neighbours began calling that little Novi Pazar. Don't misunderstand me to have anything against the people from Sandzak. Even now, I have some friends and acquaintances among them. But it wasn't normal, and it wasn't in line with the criteria of the police for large numbers of persons from that area to become police officers in the city of Sarajevo, even reserve police officers, let alone active duty. And even -- they even were appointed to the high positions in the ministry. And those were people who worked in Novi Pazar, and they were unfamiliar with the security situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. They don't know the geography and certainly didn't meet the conditions to become a senior officer in the ministry, in a very responsible position, without having earned any distinction in -- in the police before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there and ask you to please concentrate on my question and try and just answer it as shortly as possible. You gave the answer in one word, but then you went on for about 15 lines. I want to talk specifically now about these reserve policemen that you say were being hired in the dozens, Muslim citizens from Sandzak. You said they were recognised by their accent. How many of these dozens of newly hired reserve police did you talk to in order to be able to hear their accent?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm -- I'm sorry, I just have one intervention in the transcript. It was written here 48:7 that the witness said they don't know the geography. I believe -- I believe what the witness said was quite different than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, it is really non-responsive to my question. I'm satisfied to let the Defence address it in re-direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Unless you can tell me, Mr. Macar, in a short answer, what you said instead of "they don't know the geography"? Did you say something else there; and, if so, can you tell us what it is, briefly?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that they didn't know geography. I spoke about a person appointed to a high position in the ministry who didn't even know Bosnia-Herzegovina. He didn't -- wasn't aware of the problems the ministry faced, and he didn't even know a single town in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you give us some specific examples of someone fitting that description, that was appointed to a high position and didn't know the name of a single town in Bosnia? Who was that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that they did not know the name of a single town. They did not know -- they were not familiar with towns. You have to know a town in order to be familiar with the problems that are prevalent there, and this person did not know about the problems that existed in Sarajevo and yet was appointed to a high position in the Ministry of the Interior. For instance, Dazdarevic, Hasib, if I'm not mistaken, was his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But it was not a qualification, for example, to be hired as reserve policeman in Novo Sarajevo, or in Centar, in a local SJB to be from that area; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to become a reserve policemen in a SJB, one had to have permanent residence in the city of Sarajevo, or, rather, whatever the municipality was, where the reserve public security station operated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how was that permanent residence established? Did you have to have been living for there for five years before applying for a job, or five weeks, or five days? What were the rules about that, if you know.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to be registered as a permanent resident, you first had to de-register from your previous place of residence. So that was the first condition in order to be granted the residence in a certain place. And then, once the address was registered, the local public security stations ran some checks, whether this person is, indeed, residing at the registered address. And I'm sure that the files are still available and the names of the personnel are known. I think it would be an easy job to check whether those persons had de-registered from their original places of residence in Serbia and Montenegro, in order to qualify as permanent residents of Sarajevo, in order to qualify for an identity card issued in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But you, yourself, have never looked at those documents and made that check; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of my operative work, and the same goes for my immediate subordinates, inspectors who actually did the job, we received information as to how people got the jobs. I'm not now talking about all of the people, 100 per cent of them. And I would like to say that that I said in the year of 1990 and 1991, there was this huge influx of people from Sandzak who moved en masse to Sarajevo. The assessment in 1991 was that we were talking about 30.000 people. And in that period, they played the key part in elicit trade, trafficking, in other words --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Please, please stop. My question was: Have you, yourself, looked at those documents and made that check? You've answered my question, as far as I can see. I don't need the further comment. Now, it was a well-known problem about the -- I'll use the term the loading of the reserve force throughout Bosnia in late 1991. As a matter of fact, there was a commission established that included some individuals from the federal SUP that came to investigate that situation. Did you know about that commission and its work in late 1991?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that such a commission existed, but I don't know about the tasks of the commission, and I had nothing to do with it, because my post was too low. Now, let me try and give you an explanation as to the question how I actually know that someone --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No. Please. Mr. Zecevic may direct -- raise that with you on re-direct, but let me carry on because I have a time-limit. We'd like to get you out of here this week. Did you know that Mico Davidovic was a member of that commission?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I take it you didn't attend any of the meetings where that commission presented their findings to Mr. Delimustafic and Mr. Mandic and others; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was an employee of the Ministry of the Interior in the Sarajevo SUP, not in the MUP headquarters. But I didn't even receive any information to the effect that Mr. Davidovic was a member of the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I take it then the short answer would be no, you did not attend any such meetings; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Nor read any written reports produced by members of that commission; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I note the time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, so we take the break now, to return in 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, 55 more minutes. If you need to stop sooner, let us know. You mentioned in your testimony that in the summer of 1991 you became aware that certain Muslims were being recommended or sent by the SDA to Croatia for training by the Croatian MUP. Were you aware, in late 1991, early 1992, that certain Serbs were going for police-related training outside of Bosnia, certain Bosnian Serbs? Did you know anything like that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Police training, I mean regular education, was carried out in Belgrade, Skopje, and Zagreb. There were faculties and vocational colleges for police forces, and up until that time, I was unaware of the fact that any political party was sending the personnel, elected according to their standards, to undergo training outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we show the witness Exhibit 1D135.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, this will be on your screen in a moment. And I believe it's a document that you may have been shown before during the OTP's interview with you. It relates to a meeting on the 11th of February, 1992. This is tab 76 of the Prosecution's list. And this is a meeting of certain Serb members of the BiH MUP. Do you recall having been shown this document before?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a -- very inconvenient for me, the position -- the way it's positioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that better? That's just the first page. You see the list of people attending?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think one of the investigators had asked me whether I had attended the meeting in Banja Luka at the previous meeting. And you can see from this that I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. I see your name is not on the list, and I think you told us -- you told that investigator at the time that you had not been at this meeting. Did you ever hear about it? Were you ever told about it by anyone that there had been this meeting in February 1992 attended by Mr. Mico Stanisic and Zupljanin and the others listed there? Did you ever know about it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you said "not at the time." Was there a time later when you became aware of that? And I mean sometime before you were shown it by the OTP investigator in 2005 or 2006, whenever that was. Did you become aware of it sometime later in 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, maybe you and I can agree on one thing. Would you agree with me that one of the -- one of the key contributors to the breakup of the old MUP and, indeed, the breakup of old Bosnia-Herzegovina, was the role of the nationalist political parties, the SDA, the HDZ, and the SDS? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would not agree where the argument that the existence of nationalist parties per se resulted in the breakup. I would prefer to say that some individuals from those nationalist parties did things that led to the breakup of the former Yugoslavia itself, because the very fact of their existence does not yield any results. There have to be individuals who take certain action, probably as instructed by those who controlled them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. That's fair. I was trying to address it by phrasing my question just talking about the role of those parties. But I take it from your answer that we could agree that the actions of certain individuals from each of those three nationalist political parties were a key factor in the breakup. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can recall this correctly, and based on what I heard from the media, the Serbian Democratic Party in Bosnia and Herzegovina took action and agreed to take some action in the sphere of some negotiations about the status of Bosnia and Herzegovina and former Yugoslavia itself, and also negotiations about the internal structure of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I don't know that anyone from the SDS leadership - I'm now talking based on the information that I got from the media, and we all followed media very closely at the time -- that anyone took any action that resulted in the situation that we witnessed in April and later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Not aware of any actions by Mr. Karadzic, or Mr. Krajisnik, that might have contributed to what followed; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that they took action that have led to the breakup of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Based on what we could read in the media and what I knew as a citizen and as a police officer, based on the conversations with my colleagues and friends, I think that effort was made to continue talks and negotiations, in order to avoid the worst possible outcome in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you know about the activities of any SDS members in connection with arming the Serbs - and I'm talking about not Serb policemen but Serb civilians - before the breakup in early April 1992? Did you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the tasks within the purview of the city SUP, which I actually did, the service did not receive any information that any of the Serbs were arming the Serb citizenry on any basis whatsoever. And if my memory serves me right, the Serbs still believed that there was the Yugoslav People's Army as the regular armed force, and that the Ministry of the Interior existed as a regular ministry, and that it continued functioning as usual, despite the problems that were occurring by that time. And my personal opinion was that this situation, within the ministry, would be resolved, regardless of some anomalies that were apparent. Now as for the information that -- within the service, after all, a Croat man was my superior, and if he had had any knowledge about the Serbs being armed, he would have issued an order to me, because we were a mixed group, to do something about it. We would have been ordered to do something about it. There was a case where the city SUP took part in. There was some report that weapons were stored in a house belonging to a citizen in Pofalici, and there was a joint action by the relevant stations, police stations in Sarajevo and the city SUP, and it turned out that this was, in fact, false information. And a large police contingent took part in this operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we show the witness Exhibit P648. It's tab 65.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, I'll see if I have a hard copy for you. Yes, with the usher's assistance, can I hand you a hard copy. Sir, this a document dated the 20th of September, 1993. And it comes from the then-chief of Ilidza SJB, Tihomir Glavas. Did you know Mr. Glavas?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this document itself appears to be some sort of report on the activities of Ilidza SJB from -- actually, from the beginning of 1991 through the end of 1992. And recommendations of certain individuals for awards or decorations. If you could turn to page 4 in the English, it's item number 1 for Tomislav Kovac. Yeah. I'm not sure what page that is for you, but do you find the reference to Mr. Kovac? I think it --

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you know Mr. Kovac. This is Mr. Kovac who later was the assistant minister who was authorised to act for Mr. Stanisic, according to you, in October 1992. It's the same guy we're talking about; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kovac worked in the Ilidza station.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you'll see in this document, Mr. Glavas says about Mr. Kovac that he made a special contribution to preparing the Serbian people for defence, setting up the Serbian public security station, organising illegal work, and arming the Serbian people? You didn't know about that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: What period are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, before the split of the MUP in early April 1992. You didn't know about that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not know that Mr. Kovac was arming the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. With Mr. Zecevic last week, on the 5th of July, you talked about -- he asked you about some of the significant events in Sarajevo shortly before the conflict actually started in April. And you mentioned the murder of a wedding guest, and you mentioned the blockade of the 2nd Army headquarters on the 15th of March. But you didn't mention the set-up of barricades all around Sarajevo immediately after that wedding guest was murdered. You remember that, though, right? That was a big deal in Sarajevo, on the 3rd and 4th of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this period when the roadblocks were set up in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you know about the involvement of the SDS in the -- in some of those barricades that were set up?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not a member of the SDS, and I don't know what role the SDS played in the setting up of barricades. I know that in March there was a great deal of tension in the city of Sarajevo. There was a great deal of fear among the citizens. They feared for their own safety. And according to the information that I have, the barricades in Sarajevo were set up spontaneously, and now whether the SDS played any part in that, I can't really say that. I can't give you an answer because I was not familiar with what the SDS was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. And I take it -- since the creation of the new nationalist parties, have you ever been a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until 1987, I was a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia. And at my own request, I stopped being a member of that party. Until 2000, the year of 2000, I was not a member of any party.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in 2000, did you become a member of some party; if so, which one?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Party of Democratic Progress. Mladen Ivanic is the leader. And last year, I decided that I don't want to be a member anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could show the witness Exhibit P991.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't have a hard copy of this one with me at the moment, Mr. Macar, but let's first take a look at the first page. And maybe you can tell me whether or not you have ever seen it, and that will maybe shorten the exercise. This is dated the 6th of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is tab 77 on the Prosecution's list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is a report from the State Security Service in the Ministry of the Interior of the then-joint MUP. Copies to the president of the Presidency, to the assembly chairman, to the prime minister, the deputy prime ministers, and to the president of the BH Presidency Council for the preservation of constitutional order. And it is about the events of 1, 2, 3, and 4 March in Sarajevo, relating in particular to the barricades. Did you ever see this document? I understand, given the level that you were working with at the time and not being an addressee, it is likely that you did not. But can you help us?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I haven't seen it, nor did I have any special contacts with state security. Because from January or, actually, February 1992, it became obvious that the leadership of state security at the level of the Sarajevo centre, and especially at the ministry headquarters, was, in fact, the extended arm of the SDA party. Most of them, anyway. And you could tell from individual events and from some information that the service received from public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's show you another one, and I'll ask you a similar question. This is Exhibit P643. And this is tab 78 on the Prosecution's list. Mr. Macar, this is a -- this is another report relating to the barricades. This one is dated the 13th of March, 1992. And, actually, it is more focussed on the specific activities of certain MUP members. Did you ever see this report before?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, have you followed on TV or in the media the proceedings in this trial, in Mr. Mico Stanisic's trial?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very little. I don't even know if there were any direct transmissions. Only when the agency reported about this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're currently leaving in Bijeljina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We've had several former -- and maybe, I guess, some are still employed with the police. But we have had several former RS MUP personnel testify in this trial. And, I wonder, in the past year or two, have you had any conversations with anybody that you know that testified in this trial?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that I spoke to anybody about this trial. No, not about this trial. I don't really remember I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. That would have been my next question. But, first, it was just to establish if you'd spoken to anybody who testified at the trial. Do you know some of the former RS MUP employees living in Bijeljina who testified here? Mr. Vlaski? Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vlaski lives in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My mistake. Who lives in Bijeljina that used to work in the MUP, the RS MUP in 1992, when you worked there? Can you name those people for me.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who lives in Bijeljina of the people I knew from the period when I was with the MUP? Milorad Maric; and then there's Miroslav Maric, that's a different person; then there's Goran Saric; Ranko Sugalo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Anyone else at your level, that is, at the level of assistant minister or the head of an administration at MUP headquarters?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milos Zuban. Rade Radovic. There are probably more, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that just before the breakup, at the very end of March, you had a meeting in your office with your boss, Jozo Leutar. Am I pronouncing his name correctly? Do you recall having a meeting with him in your office in late March 1992 where he told you about a split of the then-existing BiH MUP?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was not in my office. Due to the complex security situation in Sarajevo, the immediate supervisors who were subordinated to Mr. Leutar used his office throughout March, and it was in his office that we had a -- that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall specifically when that meeting was? What day, what month?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in late February [as interpreted] 1992. Perhaps on the 31st.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, when you testified about it last week, at page 22.838, you initially said in late March 1991, and then you corrected yourself and said you misspoke, it was 1992. But you did say March. And now you are saying February. You said February 31st, and we all know February only has usually 28 or 29 days. So is it the 31st of March?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say February. I said March. I do know that much. And the year is 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry, I'm only reading what comes out on the English translation. Now, you've seen the next document that I'm going to show you, which is P353. Yes, it is on both the Prosecution and the Defence list. I think tab 4 for us -- for the Defence, and tab 6 for the Prosecution. This is a dispatch sent by Mr. Mandic, essentially announcing the existence of the newly created Serbian MUP in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Did you see that at the time, on the 31st of March, 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said already, this dispatch was sent to the secretary of the Sarajevo SUP and is -- if my memory serves me well, Mr. Kijac was the one. And he had regular meetings with his co-workers and his closest co-worker was Mr. Leutar because he was the head of the crime enforcement service. I don't know how long the meeting was. We were in Mr. Leutar's office. I cannot be certain if it was on the 31st or on the 30th, or maybe on the 1st of April, when I learned about the contents of the dispatch. It was read out to us. There was a Mr. Nuic present and other people, too, in Mr. Leutar's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, even if you don't recall what day it was that you might have seen it in Mr. Leutar's office, isn't it a fact that this was headline news all over town in Sarajevo? It was in all the newspapers on that day, or the very next day, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the newspapers received the dispatch before the addressees, then they would have published it, but I don't see how they could have. We see that it says DD, and urgency, so that all the addressees would have received it on the 31st of March, and the media were only in a position to report about it later, after the 31st, which means in early April. I don't believe that they were -- they had that information before. At least I don't think that they could have published information from this dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, isn't it true that sometimes dispatches like this were sent to the local media the very same day they were being sent out internally within the MUP?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You'd have to ask the media people about that. And, yes, there was leakage of information from the MUP, but whether this document leaked through somebody in the MUP is something I don't know. Bearing in mind that the MUP was already breaking up, it wouldn't surprise me to learn that some -- somebody from the MUP, indeed, related the contents of dispatch to the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We'll look at some other dispatches in a little bit. But I want to ask you whether it was the 31st of March, or the 1st of April, or the 3rd of April, I think you mentioned, when you learned about the contents of this dispatch. It wasn't a surprise for you, Mr. Macar, was it, because you had already heard about the creation of the new Serbian MUP of the Serbian Republic of BiH on the 30th of March, in Sokolac, when you saw Mr. Stanisic addressing those policemen under Mr. Zoran Cvijetic; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was present in Sokolac. And as I've already said, I was familiar with everything that happened at the stadium and the information that was disclosed to me then. Just like Mr. Leutar, when he paraphrased this dispatch that he had received and he told me that in Mostar the technical preconditions were created and that they also had staff and everything necessary for the functioning of the Croatian MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned at - what do we call it? - the parade of the police in Sokolac, on the 30th, that Mr. Milorad Maric was also there. And tell us again, he was the chief of Ilijas SJB at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was he from Sokolac, too?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was standing where I was standing, too. And there were other citizens. Yes, he was in Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand he was there. But my question was: Was he from Sokolac, like you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't. He was from Ilijas.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know how he happened to be in Sokolac on that day for this parade? Did he have some advance notice of it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were members of the Ilijas SJB at that parade, too. To the best of my recollection, there were also representatives of Pale, Sokolac, and other municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And by that, I take it you mean uniformed policemen who were participating in the parade. Is that -- is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a review of the uniformed police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you personally know any of these uniformed policemen from the other SJBs, like Pale and Ilijas?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew Mr. Maric because he used to work at the Sarajevo Centar SUP. I think he was assistant commander or deputy commander. And I held a position there at one time, too. I knew Mr. Koroman, whom I had met in a previous period concerning some events in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So Malko Koroman was there, too? I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember it correctly. I think I saw him in the video-clip, but in order to be fully certain, I would have to see it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I was thinking the same thing, that maybe we could show you the video. But I will leave that for tomorrow when I have more time to set up the video. Now, tell me, how did you first become aware that this event was going to be happening on that day? I think March 30th in 1992 was a Monday. How did you find out about it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that a few days before the 15th, that's when it was I believe, that my late wife and I took our daughters to my parents at Sokolac. One went to kindergarten, and the other went to primary school, but neither kindergartens nor schools functioning anymore in town, and the situation was bad. My wife worked at the Ministry of Finance of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We decided that we should take our children to my parents, and we were carrying some clothes and stuff, and on one day when I was in Sokolac, we learned the news that there would be this parade at the stadium in Sokolac. After this parade, like everybody else, including police officers, I was interested. And I had the opportunity to speak to Mr. Stanisic briefly. He explained to me that, pursuant to a decision taken by the Assembly of the Serbian People and in accordance with the Cutileiro Plan, this was done. And I was interested in the further developments. In the framework of the ministries, in order to co-ordinate work at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina, steps would be taken to overcome the blockade of the work of the MUP. I can state with full responsibility that in early January, at least in Sarajevo, the functioning of the entire ministry was --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Macar.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- blocked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Please. Please. My question was: How did you find out about it, and you're going a little beyond that. Your answer was translated as, page 65, line 20: "I've already said that a few days before the 15th ..." Did you mean -- did they hear you and translate you correctly? Did you mean before the 30th of March, rather than the 15th?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained that maybe a few days before the 15th of March, my late wife and I took the children to Sokolac. And, on the last weekend in March, when we were staying at my parents' house to visit our children, I learned that at the stadium in Sokolac, it was a stadium or pitch of the local sports club, there would be this police parade. That's what I have just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. What I'm trying to find out is specifically how you found out and when you found out. Did you find out on the day before, on the 29th of March, or on Saturday, the 28th? And who told you about it? Or did you read it somewhere? How did you find out, and from whom, and when?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If my memory serves me well, I heard that news from Mr. Zoran Cvijetic, whom I met in one of the restaurants at Sokolac. And the restaurant is near the family-owned shop where I used to go rather often to have coffee and meet some acquaintances from Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to use the video with this witness to cover a few more matters relating to this. I know we're ten minutes early, but given he has had some physical discomfort today, it would be convenient for me - it won't make my cross-examination go into a new day, whether that is Thursday or Friday - just that ten minutes won't make that difference, I promise, if we can recess now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we take the adjournment now, to resume tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 12th day of July, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.36 p.m.,
